## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (a still ride, a joke, a long camp routine, a long confession, a quiet close). Voice Differentiation Strong (Taerel's formal wit, Aymir's soldier humour, Lysana's dryness, Luca's two registers), Moderate where Taerel and Lysana pick up modern words. Stress Escalation Moderate (the pressure is the confession). World Texture Strong (the stew, the salting, the oiled cloth, the rifle). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong (Lysana's hand, Aymir's look away). Prose Control Moderate (the negation turns and the "the way" explanations).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 14 to 16. Those chapters are fights and rescues and this chapter slows to a camp and lets one man tell a story. The telling is the longest single speech in the book so far and it holds. The shift in Luca's voice from slang ("ain't", "gonna") to formal when he begins is a choice that works.

**POP** Luca yes, strongly (his two registers). Aymir yes (the cursed elk). Taerel yes (Perish the thought entirely). Lysana yes (the goat scream, the hand at the glove).

**AI** Moderate. The tells are six negation turns in the narration, two blades, several stock closers, and a "the way" explanation. The dialogue is clean and Luca's telling is the book's best.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line, ran the mechanical net, and checked Zac's find in paragraph 107 and the Pearl ruling in paragraph 109 first. The camp routine is kept as a deliberate delay. Paragraph numbers match line numbers in this chapter (there are no blank lines between paragraphs). I checked against the canon ledger (Pearl, Tafeld, Ariel, the Night Veil, Jasper and Adin), the Editor Packet options, and the voice anchors for Luca, Taerel, Aymir and Lysana.

# Chapter 21


## First impression

This is the book's heist chapter, and it has the right pulse. A cramped room, a plan nobody is sure of, and then three tight scenes in the dark (Nyssa and Weslin in the alley, Ash alone with his flasks, Weslin at the ward). Nyssa and Weslin are the warmest pair in it ("Repetition keeps the screaming quiet", "Nope. Just true."). Ash's solo is the best character work, since he starts with a plan, hears a gut itch, climbs through an unmarked hatch and finds a room of explosives with "aren't you just asking to be set on fire?". Weslin finally gets to use what Aurelia taught him, and the quiet "Thanks" to whoever is listening pays it off. The chapter is also where the Ch19 rift with Aurelia is answered, since she is the one who worries aloud about putting him in danger. What weakens it is the setup room and a few tangled passages. The headcount (seven figures, nine named), the dismissed Dain who is then addressed, the link that goes to "each of them" and then only to Weslin, and Nyssa's speech with narration inside the quote marks are all fixable in a line each. The last of the three is the worst, since two sentences of Weslin's inner life are spoken by Nyssa. Paragraph 92 is a garble. The vocabulary slips toward modern (tactical armor, utility junction, concrete). The Zac find in paragraph 78 is logged as Option A.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (a still room, a quick alley, a long solo, a short ward). Voice Differentiation Strong for Nyssa, Ash and Weslin, Moderate for Harmon and Garr, Weak for Dain (no line). Stress Escalation Strong (every scene tightens). World Texture Strong (the lute slurred by ale and apathy, the tannery, the grease trap). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong (Aurelia's worry, Nyssa's wish for Dain, Weslin's thanks). Prose Control Moderate (a few garbled passages and modern words).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 17 and 19. Chapter 17 plans, Chapter 19 argues and Chapter 21 goes in. This is the "execute" beat of the book's plan, brief, execute, adapt cadence. It is cleaner than Chapter 16 and shorter than the sections of Chapter 15. The three-scene shape (alley, Ash, Weslin) is the right one, since each scene has a different kind of tension.

**POP** Nyssa yes, strongly. Ash yes, strongly. Weslin yes. Garr yes in two lines. Aurelia yes in one. Aldrek yes in chains. Dain no line.

**AI** Moderate. The tells are stock similes at transitions (night's cloak, silent as a shadow, as if drawing breath), a few negation fragments, and told closers. The dialogue is clean.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line, ran the mechanical net and the italics check (the telepathy lines in paragraphs 80 and 82), and checked Zac's find in paragraph 78 first. Paragraph numbers are non-empty paragraphs (the blank lines between the early paragraphs shift the mechanical counts). I checked against Chapters 17 to 19 (the plan, the link, the clock), the canon ledger (Aldrek, Ash, the prisoners, the staged arrest) and the voice anchors for Nyssa, Ash, Weslin and Aldrek.

# Chapter 22


## First impression

This is the breach and it moves. Aldrek sits in the interrogation room being a quiet heretic, the first boom shakes the dust, and from there the chapter is a descent. Four floors, each with its own texture (the keys and the Warden's office, the stacked wards, the cell menagerie on the third level, the vault on the fourth), a fight that Ash walks into on purpose, and then a reveal. Ash is the star. "That one was mine", "Third surprise. I might've set fire to your artillery shed" and "I need the practice" give him the best run of dialogue in the book. The cell menagerie (the Joblin who waves, the man who needs no air, the Orth) is the strongest world texture in the chapter and it earns its space. Weslin gets his first real mistake, the missed ward, and the link to Aurelia is severed, which raises the stakes for the rest of the book. The reveal of Dain in a guard's uniform pays off Nyssa's wish from Chapter 21. What holds it back is a handful of tangles. The interrogation opens mid-answer, with Aldrek replying to a question the officer has not yet asked. Paragraph 23 is garbled. Weslin is described as tall and adult. Weslin explains his training to Ash at a length no scared fourteen-year-old would manage. The chapter has five interrupted lines marked with a dash, which the house rule does not allow. Ash says in Chapter 21 that Dain is outside the walls, and Dain turns up inside the prison.

# Chapter 23


## First impression

This is the payoff chapter for the prison arc and it plays like one. Dain's tackle by Aldrek is a good opening beat, and "Improvisation. Your tackle was appreciated. Brought the role together" is the best Dain line so far. The rescue itself is brisk. Weslin disarms two wards in a row and grows into it, the reunion with Riven carries a charge that Dain notices and Weslin wisely looks away from, and Torrek and Haldrin get just enough on the page to be remembered. The courtyard exit works because the fire gives the cover and Dain sells the voice. Neavin popping out of the fountain with a score for Ash's explosion is the right release before the last scene. Then Harmon, three Forged and the collapse, which is the real hook of the chapter. The kills are fast and cinematic, and the armor vanishing on the word "horse" is a strong image. What holds it back is small. Dain's account of the drainage tunnel contradicts what the team just walked through, Riven is a "brother" in the dialogue and something more in the embrace, the new prisoners are called "the new guy" for two men, and the collar on Torrek is never dealt with. Two stock similes also sit in an otherwise clean action scene.

# Chapter 24


## First impression

This is the book's first long look at the court, and it is a good change of air after the prison. The Accord feast has real texture (Vaugre and the pearls, the peacocks and the lion, deals dancing as much as feet), Edric is warm and public and sure of himself, and the quiet cut to Drake in the corridor is the best beat in the chapter. The threat with the velvet pouch and the lock of hair is cold and specific, and Drake taking a breath to put the mask back on is exactly the right restraint. Merrick's rage scene is a strong swing, a man who built himself out of the gutter watching it slip, with the bounty list and the half-remembered Emberlight lord as the sting. The Queen's bedchamber scene gives a clean plant (the guards barely checked the carts) and the watcher on the roof closes the chapter with the right chill. What holds it back is a heavier hand of stock lines (the world on his shoulders, wine like a river, the veins bulging), an unclear alliance in the corridor (who does Cotter serve, and what is Drake hiding about Merrick), a report from Jerric that contradicts itself, and a batch of small mechanical slips, including six uses of the wrong name for Cotter.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (feast, private council, corridor, balcony, Merrick's rage, bedchamber, rooftop). Voice Differentiation Strong for Vaugre, Drake, Edric, Mirelle and Merrick, Moderate for Jerric (his report contradicts itself). Stress Escalation Strong (the pouch, the note, the bounty, the watcher). World Texture Strong (the Accord, the Hall of the Griffin, the Syrellian ash dish). Sensory Grounding Moderate to Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong (Drake's mask, the Queen's dread). Prose Control Moderate (a heavier run of stock lines in the second half).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 20 to 23. After three action chapters in a row this is the first quiet one, and it is the right size. It works as a "brief" beat for the court side of the book, setting the Accord, Merrick's reaction and a new plant for the Queen. It is more talk-heavy than Chapter 23 and carries more plot.

**POP** Edric yes. Drake yes, strongly. Cotter yes in one cold scene. Merrick yes, as a man who built himself out of the gutter. Mirelle yes. The watcher yes as a silhouette.

**AI** Moderate. The tells are not-X-but-Y turns (paragraphs 10, 54, 107, 114), stock similes (12, 45, 65), and abstract closers (58, 94). The dialogue is clean apart from Drake's line in 43 and Jerric's report in 78.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line, ran the mechanical net, the italics check and the Zac notes. The Cotter name fix (six places) is logged in the first item, and the simile note to keep "Not the way they should have." is honoured. I compared against the canon ledger (Merrick, the Iron Flask, Dain's cover, Stormhold in the open decisions) and the voice anchors for Edric and Drake.

# Chapter 25


## First impression

Taerel finally takes the mask off, and the first half is the best of the chapter. The reveal is staged well, with Aymir giving him the nudge, the horses stopping, the face gone with no ceremony, and Lysana's "You could have warned a girl before you turned into a walking night sky" landing the laugh. Luca not flinching and Aymir's "Told you he was dramatic" keep it light, and the brother explanation gives Aymir and Taerel a real history. The second half is a recon chapter, and it is competent. The camp is well drawn (the tar, the forge smoke, the totem, the staff that matches the last one), Luca's urge to strike and Lysana's "No" is a clean character beat, and "Orcs don't do siege warfare" is the right alarm. But the chapter is long for what it does. The team counts the camp, reports it, scouts again, counts it again, reports it again, and asks twice how to reach the survivors. The rotation plan is given twice, the careful-not-blunder line is said by four people, and the closing paragraph is a prophecy line the chapter does not need. Taerel also slips into a modern register in two lines, and there is a run of small mechanical breaks, including a paragraph split mid-sentence.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Moderate (reveal, ride, overlook, scouting, scouting again). Voice Differentiation Strong for Lysana, Aymir and Luca, Moderate for Taerel (two modern lines). Stress Escalation Moderate (the second half repeats its beats). World Texture Strong (the totem, the forge smoke, the staffs, the chapel). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong in the first half, Moderate in the second. Prose Control Moderate (a paragraph split, stray marks and stock similes).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 15 to 24. This is the "brief" beat after the prison and the court, and it is the first time Luca's team is the point of view since Chapter 20. The reveal is the strongest single scene since the Chapter 20 telling, and the siege half is longer than it needs to be. It runs the same length as Chapter 22 and carries about half the plot.

**POP** Lysana yes, strongly. Aymir yes. Taerel yes in the reveal, no in two modern lines. Luca yes in his "No" scene.

**AI** Light to Moderate. The tells are stacked similes in the first two paragraphs, a run of told emotion (paragraphs 65, 87, 107, 134), and an abstract closer in paragraph 158. The dialogue is clean, apart from Taerel's register and the echo in paragraphs 109 to 111.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line, ran the mechanical net, and checked there were no stored Zac notes for this chapter. I compared Taerel's lines against his voice anchor (formal, dry, no Hey or Figured), Aymir's against his (educated, soldier-buddy humor) and Lysana's against hers, and checked the bracelet against Chapter 21's link question. I checked the staff against the earlier orc camp.

# Chapter 26


## First impression

This is a quieter, tighter chapter than 25 and it earns its length. It opens inside Aymir's head with a smell, and the burning oil sends him back to a war the reader has not seen, which is the best use of Aymir so far. Taerel's knuckle against his arm is the right gesture, and the bet about the worg is the right way out of it. The arrow with the note is Lysana's idea, built from what is on the page (the volleys, the quiver, the cloth), and the answer from the church in dyed bedding flags is a clean payoff. The farewell between the brothers is the emotional center, with the coin, the two ritual lines and "tell Dad I tried", and it works because nobody explains it. The closing flag message and "Thank you, God the Creator" give the chapter a real exit. What holds it back is small. The chapter changes place and time four times with no scene break, the church was a chapel in Chapter 25, the dialogue has two voice slips (Taerel's "Hey" and Lysana asking Aymir to explain his rifle for the reader), a handful of stock similes sit in the weather paragraphs, and the last line sends Taerel off with a cliche.

Voice Differentiation Strong for Lysana, Luca and Aymir, Moderate for Taerel (one casual opener). Stress Escalation Strong (the oil, the sealed routes, the wait for an answer). World Texture Strong (the signal flags, the waxed cloth, the Fennar method). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong (Aymir's flashback, the brothers' ritual, the unspoken thing between Luca and Lysana). Prose Control Moderate (missing breaks, a few stock similes).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 22 to 25. After the reveal and the long recon of Chapter 25, this is the better-paced half of the same assignment. It shows the "adapt" beat well, since the team cannot get in, tries something, and gets an answer. It is shorter than Chapter 25 and carries more feeling.

**POP** Aymir yes, strongly. Lysana yes, as the one with the idea. Luca yes in two quiet beats. Taerel yes in the farewell and the coin.

**AI** Light. The tells are a few stock similes (paragraphs 1, 36, 38, 77), an abstract adjective in paragraph 5, and a cliche closer in paragraph 93. The dialogue is clean apart from the two voice slips in paragraphs 19 and 79.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line, ran the mechanical net, and checked that there were no stored Zac notes for it. I compared Taerel's lines against his voice anchor, and the church against Chapter 25's chapel. I left the line in paragraph 91, "Thank you, God the Creator", exactly as written, per the God stays rule.

# Chapter 27


## First impression

This is the book's first long exhale, and it is written like one. After the prison, the ride and the rescue, the camp is quiet and everyone is carrying something. Garr turning the messages face down on the table is the best single gesture in the chapter, because it shows the cost of command without a word of narration. Weslin's lesson with Aurelia is tender and well paced, with the candle failing once and then holding, and "Safe" as his one-word answer. Dain and Garr in the middle section give both men a real wound, and Dain's "Not everything has to stay broken" to Nyssa is the right size of hope. The stew scene is warm and funny, Calen's thank-you lands, and Haldrin's tale of the Veylnar and the Pearl gives the reader the lore as a story the fire has to hold. Then Harmon walks out of the dark and corrects the tale. That is a great chapter ending. What holds it back is repetition and a handful of continuity slips. Garr's weight of command is told six times. Torrek is "pale and wiry" here and massive in Chapter 23. Dain quotes lines Garr never said. The chapter changes place three times with no scene break, and the plural "gods" sits in a chapter the packet says already says God the Creator.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the sickroom, the lesson, the walk, the arrival, the stew, the tale, the entrance). Voice Differentiation Strong for Garr, Dain, Aurelia, Ash and Riven, Moderate for Neavin (no dialect). Stress Escalation Moderate (the stakes are internal until the last page). World Texture Strong (the Veylnar tale, True Eyes, the signal in the dark). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong (the face-down messages, Dain's loss, Calen's thanks). Prose Control Moderate (a heavy run of told weight in Garr's scenes, several fragments and slogans).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 22 to 26. After the long prison arc and the siege recon, this is the first chapter with the whole company in one place, and it earns the stillness. It closes the "adapt" beat with a regroup and opens a new "plan" beat by waking Harmon. It is shorter in plot than Chapter 25 and heavier in feeling.

**POP** Garr yes, strongly. Weslin yes. Aurelia yes. Dain yes, in both of his scenes. Ash yes in two lines. Nyssa yes, briefly. Riven yes in one line. Harmon yes, with an entrance.

**AI** Light to Moderate. The tells are a run of told weight in Garr's interior, stock phrases (too quiet, the silence doing the work, swallowed whole), fragment labels (paragraphs 78 and 98) and slogans (paragraphs 25 and 81). The dialogue is clean apart from Neavin's missing dialect and Dain's reported speech.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line, ran the mechanical net and checked the stored Zac notes first. The Torn and Forgehallow fixes and the two Keep and no-change rulings (Garr's toll line, the ordered logs line) are honoured. I compared Torrek, Haldrin, Neavin and Dain against Chapter 23 and the canon ledger, and the Veylnar tale against the ledger's Council of Seven. I left the plural gods line alone and logged it as a question.

# Chapter 28


## First impression

This is a talking chapter, and it is one of the strongest in the book because every conversation moves someone. Harmon is back and the first thing he does is thank Garr and Dain, then take Garr aside and make him promise not to tell Weslin about the ring. That is the cost of command in two paragraphs. The debriefs after it are quick and each one gives a different freedom. Torrek wants to disappear, Haldrin wants his work, Riven gets a pardon and tells Harmon he joined for her, and the reveal that Calen is Reau, the son of Harmon's old friend Arthur, with a binding collar and a stolen sword hanging in Merrick's house, is the best surprise since the prison. Harmon's "Good lad" to Weslin and the morning pack-up with Aurelia's "little flame" close it softly. What holds it back is that the chapter repeats itself more than it needs to. Harmon tells the camp to rest and then to wait for the new blood three times. The camp is shown breaking up in four separate passages. Harmon says twice that he waited to see if Riven would run. Several lines are garbled, Torn's name is still Tarn, the speech marks wander between straight and curly in about seventy places, and a few continuity threads need Zac, including the armor Harmon straps on a morning after it vanished, the collar nobody mentioned in Chapter 23, and whether Reau's father is dead.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (a debrief, the ring, four interviews, a night's work, the morning). Voice Differentiation Strong for Harmon, Riven, Torrek, Reau and Aurelia, Moderate for Haldrin (his lines are short). Stress Escalation Moderate (the stakes are in what is said, and Reau's reveal is the spike). World Texture Strong (the pardon, the collar, the sword on display). Sensory Grounding Moderate. Emotional Subtext Strong (Garr and Harmon, Reau and his father, Riven and Nyssa). Prose Control Moderate (a heavy run of mixed marks, a few garbled lines, and repeated beats).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 22 to 27. After the prison, the court and the siege, this is the book's first full "brief" chapter, and it carries the most plot per page since the Chapter 20 telling. It resolves Harmon's wake, the five prisoners, and Garr's command, and it sets Stormhaven as the next stop. It is about the length of Chapter 27 and denser.

**POP** Harmon yes, strongly. Reau yes. Riven yes. Torrek yes in one scene. Haldrin yes in one scene. Aurelia yes. Garr yes in the ring scene. Weslin yes in two beats.

**AI** Light. The tells are a few stock similes (paragraphs 2, 21, 42, 54), a repeated stock phrase (paragraph 15), and a run of told closers (paragraphs 116, 140, 141, 156). The dialogue is clean apart from the repeated order in paragraphs 28 to 40.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line, ran the mechanical net and checked the stored Zac notes first. The Torn fix, the three simile rulings (two replacements and one Keep) and the God the Creator blessing in paragraph 129 are honoured; I left the blessing alone. I compared the five prisoners against Chapters 23 and 27, the ring against the locked facts, Arthur against the Adin lock, and Merrick's seat against the ledger.

# Chapter 29


## First impression

This is the cleanest action chapter since the prison, and it belongs to Taerel. A lone rider on a frozen ridge, a bad ankle, a rock and a length of twine for a trap, seven bandits and a rifle that coughs once into the wind. It reads like a tight short story inside the larger book, with a clear want (supplies for the people behind the walls), a clear plan, a clean execution, a price paid, and a payoff that is a hug and a pair of lines. "Letting bone and tendon settle into a lie that would hold for a few more minutes" is the best sentence in the chapter, and "I got what I could" followed by Aymir's cracked "I know" is the right size of reunion. The weak spots are small. The motive is stated four times in the first half. The weather changes between paragraphs. The civilians are behind the fortress walls here and in the ruined town in Chapter 25. A dangling "It" opens the crossbow paragraph, the injury and the loot are told a little twice, and the ending reaches for a stock close. There are only a few mechanical slips.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the ride, the fall, the watching, the trap, the fight, the chase, the reunion). Voice Differentiation Strong for Taerel and Aymir. Stress Escalation Strong (the ankle, the wait, the shot, the chase). World Texture Moderate to Strong (the mask, the twine, the bandit caravan). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong (the reunion). Prose Control Moderate (stated motive, a few stock similes and a dangling pronoun).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 25 to 28. After the talk-heavy Chapter 28, this is the book's tightest solo action chapter and the first to centre Taerel as a point-of-view character. It runs the "execute" beat in miniature. It is shorter than Chapter 28 and carries one clear job.

**POP** Taerel yes, strongly. Aymir yes in the reunion. The bandits are fine as a threat, with one glance as a plant.

**AI** Light. The tells are a handful of stock similes (paragraphs 20 and 47), a half-and-half tic, and abstract glosses (paragraphs 35 and 55). The dialogue is short and clean.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line, ran the mechanical net, and checked that there were no stored Zac notes for it. I compared the survivors' position against Chapters 25 and 26, Taerel's ankle against the previous chapters, and the weather against its own paragraphs. I left the oath "By God's bread" in paragraph 61 as written, per the God stays rule.

# Chapter 30


## First impression

This is the quiet chapter of the Pass thread, and it is the one that has to make the Luca and Lysana romance land before Chapter 40 takes her. The tunnel descent is well staged (the hidden gap, the chimney-effect joke, the false-collapse ceiling, the fork, the rotten scaffold, the hatch that buckles) and the two leads finally sound like two people instead of a plan and a blade. Luca's contract story and Lysana's camp story are the heart of it, and the line "People don't talk to weapons" is the best thing in the chapter. The weak spots are the usual ones. The tunnel is described as a body (throat, jaw) three times, the emotion is told after it has already been shown, the closing exchange stacks fragments, and a Gabriel for Ariel slip sits in the middle of the best speech. The chapel ending sets the stakes cleanly and hands the next chapter its job.

# Chapter 31


## First impression

This is the regroup chapter, and it does its job well. The team is whole again, the cavern becomes a base, Taerel's wound and Aymir's report give the poison plan a believable root, and the banter (the jerky older than his humor, the tyrants, the "shadow") finally lets four people sound like a squad. Aymir's report of the orcs sitting down to eat in formation is the best beat, because it is a thing seen and not a thing explained, and the poison idea grows out of it in the right order. The trouble is the numbers. Taerel's account of how he got hurt does not match Chapter 29, the headcount of the chapel has drifted again, and the narration slips into other heads twice. The tunnel and cave are given body images again (wound, throat, veins), and a few lines tell the feeling after the scene has shown it. The chapter closes on the plan and on the right line for Aymir.

# Chapter 32


## First impression

This is the book's best city chapter so far, and the reason is restraint. Stormhaven is not shown by crowds or battle. It is shown by what is missing (no rats, no beggars, no noise), by one woman sweeping a clean stoop, and by one man in a blue tunic who drops like a cut string and is stood back up on his corner. That jerk is the scariest thing in the chapter, and Weslin's one word for it, "correction", is the right word. The entry through the smugglers' shaft and the Underlane gives Riven his home ground and a reason to be gloomy about it, the team banter keeps its edge, and the curfew bells land like a door closing. The weak spots are repeats. Riven's report says again what the chapter has already shown, the "not X, not Y" device runs three times in a few pages, Neavin and Dain slip out of their voices once each, the minutes between "dark" and "running out of light" do not agree, and Weslin's relay from Luca leaves out the plan he says Luca has. The ending is strong, though the last line has been used before.

# Chapter 33


## First impression

This is the team-up chapter before the Stormhaven missions split, and it has a lot of heart. The banter between Dain and Nyssa is the best of its kind in the book, the dress and the garter of knives are a character reveal and not just a gag, and Reau's two scenes with Weslin are the strongest in the chapter. His warning about the ring ("the ring comes first") and the collar are real plants, and Aurelia's shield lesson gives the book a rule it will need when the mind-control reveal arrives. Harmon and Garr on the way out are good for the first half, with the cane that is not for walking and the line about "ghosts in our pockets". The problems are mostly bookkeeping. The pairs Harmon names in the loft are not the pairs who leave, Dain and Nyssa leave twice, Aldrek prays three times, the cane appears before it is picked up, Harmon gives the meeting order three times, and the closing talk with Garr slides into aphorism and meta-commentary. Chapter 34 gets the same care as this one, because the stored simile note for this chapter is in Chapter 34's text.

# Chapter 34


## First impression

This is the investigation chapter, and it is the best use of the occupied city so far. Four pairs go out and each one comes back with a piece of the same shape. The boutique gives the tea invitation that smells like a trap, the blind man gives the warning that the nobles are gone though their voices walk, the apothecary and the temple woman give the name Korr and the way it slides out of the mind, and Tevin gives the best beat of the chapter when the name takes his memory in front of Riven and Ash and he closes the door smiling. The name that cannot be held is a fresh and frightening device, and it works because every witness behaves a little differently. Dain and Nyssa carry the opening on charm, Neavin and Aldrek and Aurelia get the temple with its scrubbed plaques, and Riven's history with Tevin is a strong thread. The weak spots are in the plumbing. Reau counts sources he could not have seen, Tevin tells the same story twice, the shop is reached twice, several characters drop their contractions and sound like a report, and a few places explain what the scene already shows. The ending, with the note that says not to trust what people say, especially me, is the right close.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the walk, the shop, the bar, the street, the temple, the tunnels, the door). Voice Differentiation Strong for Dain, Nyssa, Riven, Ash and Tevin, Moderate for Weslin and Neavin where the contractions go. Stress Escalation Strong (the shop's trap, the temple woman's collapse, the name that wipes a mind). World Texture Strong (the Smokeslip, the plaques in the temple, the sunburst symbol, the Sewer Valve 13 map). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong (the apothecary's song, Riven and Tevin, the smiling reset). Prose Control Moderate (a few stock similes, a few repeats, and the contractions).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 20 to 33. After the setup of Chapter 33, this is the book's first full day of investigation in Stormhaven and the first chapter that moves every Stormhaven pair at once. It is the longest chapter in the Stormhaven thread and the first to introduce the Korr name on the page.

**POP** Dain and Nyssa yes, strongly. Riven and Ash yes, strongly. Reau and Weslin yes. Neavin, Aldrek and Aurelia yes in the temple. Tevin yes, strongly, as a new character with a past. Teck, Madrelis and Halvayne work as short roles.

**AI** Light to moderate. The tells are the stacked personifications in paragraph 1, two stock closers (paragraphs 61 and 127), told emotion (paragraph 305) and the flat uncontracted dialogue. The dialogue elsewhere is sharp.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line, ran the mechanical net, and applied the stored simile Find from Chapter 33's notes, which sits in paragraph 45 of this chapter. I checked the names against the canon ledger. Sythrael Korr, Halvayne, Tevin and Liora are in it. Madrelis, Celairyn Silks, Teck, Smokeslip, the Undercircle, Duskwalk, Breachwell, Henrick's Remedies, the Temple of the Shining Oath, Ironmarch Plaza and Selenmar are new and are logged for the ledger. I did not state who or what Korr is, per the open decision. The file has no chapter heading, which the ledger also records. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule.

# Chapter 35


## First impression

This is the long, braided chapter of the Stormhaven day, and it has the book's best images so far, set against its most tangled bookkeeping. Weslin's push through the shard is the strongest scene in it, with a silence that is gone and not hushed, a surge, a breath and a masked figure that turns. The tower where five citizens walk a circle, the tea garden with the six chairs, "It's in the water", and the lemoncake exit are all sharp and in tone. Dain's speech about his sister's name gives him a reason to be the way he is. The war-beast cradle at the end earns its "declaration" through the details of fuse coils and blood channels. The trouble is repetition and offstage recaps. The trio meets the same scrubbing, scratching, forgetting worshipper in one chapter that Chapter 34 gave them already, and then a third sanctum with a boy. Dain and Nyssa visit a second boutique that the recap treats as the first. The recap lists events that are not on the page. The count of chairs, the capital, the name Albrecht, and the steel Garr reaches for and does not have all need a pass. The prose leans on "held breath" three times and on jaws and lungs for buildings. Underneath all that, the chapter has a strong spine and the ending is clean.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the plaza, the sanctum, the chase, the shard, the boutique, the tea, the cradle, the alley). Voice Differentiation Strong for Dain, Nyssa, Reau, Weslin and Halvayne, Moderate for Garr and Harmon in the proverb lines. Stress Escalation Strong (the fight at the plaza, the chase, the shard push, the garden, the war-beast). World Texture Strong (the plinths, the circling tower, the ledger of names, the cradle). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong in Dain's speech and the tea table. Prose Control Moderate (the held-breath tic, body images for buildings, and the proverb run).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 20 to 34. After the day of separate investigations in Chapter 34, this is the book's biggest Stormhaven chapter and the first to show the four threads converge. It is the longest chapter so far in the Stormhaven thread and carries the most plot. It runs the "execute" and "adapt" beats in one pass, with the war-beast as the turn.

**POP** Dain, Nyssa, Reau, Weslin and Halvayne yes, strongly. Garr and Harmon yes. Aurelia, Neavin and Aldrek yes, with the sanctum scenes the weakest. The nobles at the tea work well as a hall of horrors.

**AI** Moderate. The tells are the repeated held-breath simile, body images for buildings (jaws, lungs), the proverb run, not-X turns (paragraphs 3 to 5, 307 and 320) and told emotion (paragraph 181). The dialogue is clean where it is plain.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line, ran the mechanical net, and applied Zac's stored notes (Nysaa to Nyssa, Eastmere to Estmere, and the heading, which the chapter file does not carry). I compared the sanctum scenes against Chapter 34, the shop against Chapter 34, Weslin's shard against Chapters 33 and 34, and the steel order against Chapter 33. I checked the names against the canon ledger. Rusk, Callem Vire, Lioren, Vanneth, Varin and the New Flame are in it, while Albrecht, Vellith, Morenna, the Eastern Faith Circle and the Loyalty Test are new and are logged for it. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule.

# Chapter 36


## First impression

This is the stable-loft night, the regroup after the Stormhaven day, and it holds the book's cleanest statement of its own mystery. Harmon's "Stormhaven didn't fall. It was overwritten." is the best line in it, and Aldrek's "built over a prison" and Reau's "it won't defend, it'll lead" are close behind. The Dain and Riven flare-up has real heat and costs both men something. Weslin's guilt after the shard push is handled gently, with Reau as the anchor and Aurelia unsure how to be one. The note on the doorframe and the mirror call with Edric and Drake turn the night into a clock, which is what the chapter needs. The weakness is repetition. Harmon asks his three questions, the team answers them, and then Harmon asks them again as a "second pass" and the team answers them again, with the vision, the old woman, the tea, the loops and the unseen governor all restated. Several details also collide with other chapters, among them the governor, the war-beast chamber, the masked figure that "saw" Weslin and then did not, and the king's surname. The prose leans on bones, shadows and "not X, but Y" turns when the dialogue is already doing the work.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Moderate (the long debrief middle sags between the loft arrival and the note). Voice Differentiation Strong for Dain, Riven, Nyssa, Aldrek and Harmon, Moderate for Aurelia and Neavin in the report lines. Stress Escalation Strong (the shove, the note, the mirror call). World Texture Strong (the vault plans, the statue key, the sealed chamber). Sensory Grounding Moderate (snow, straw and lamp early, thinner in the middle). Emotional Subtext Strong in Weslin's guilt and in the Dain and Riven fight. Prose Control Moderate (the repeated debrief, the bone and shadow closers, the not-X turns).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 30 to 35. After the long braided days, this chapter slows to a debrief, and it is the first to give the reader a ticking clock. It runs the "brief" and "adapt" beats, with the note and the mirror call as the turn. It is the shortest of the Stormhaven chapters in action and the longest in talk.

**POP** Harmon, Riven, Dain, Nyssa and Aldrek yes, strongly. Weslin and Reau yes. Aurelia, Neavin, Garr and Ash yes, with Garr and Ash thin. King Edric and Drake read as functions more than people.

**AI** Light to Moderate. The tells are the bone and shadow closers, the not-X turns (paragraphs 18 and 153), the narrator that announces the second pass (paragraph 161), and one jargon list in Dain's mouth (paragraph 166). The dialogue is clean where it is plain.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line, ran the mechanical net, and applied Zac's stored notes (Wyman to Wymark in paragraphs 280 and 288, and the heading, which the chapter file does not carry). The note names "Adldrek", which does not occur in this chapter file. I compared the war-beast chamber, the old woman, the shard and the governor against Chapters 34 and 35 and the canon ledger, and logged Drake's first name as the open decision OD-2 without deciding it. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule.

# Chapter 37


## First impression

This is the cavern-camp chapter, and after two crowded Stormhaven chapters it breathes. It is also the first chapter where the Pass team gets to be funny, and it earns it. "Chivalry. Dead and buried." and "Hope he dances better than he flirts" land because the people saying them are tired and fond of each other. The structure is clean. A supply cart arrives, Taerel reads the orc camp as staged, Lysana and Aymir follow a cart into a tunnel that should not exist, they find a Joblin hub and eight unmarked riders, and Luca lays out a poisoning plan at dusk. Taerel's wish for "a back door through the mountains" pays off a few pages later, which is how a planted line should work. The problems are small and mostly about bookkeeping. Aymir is in the cavern at midday and on the trail at the same hour. The four vials are a glob, a powder, a vial and a vial. Brehn is named before he is introduced. The prose reaches for blood, embers, mouths and breathing in places where the scene is already working. The ending line is a slogan.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the cavern, the ridge, the tunnel, the chamber, the plan). Voice Differentiation Strong for Taerel, Luca, Lysana and Aymir, with the banter doing most of the work. Stress Escalation Moderate (the creature fight is the only fight, and the plan carries the tension). World Texture Strong (the Joblin hub, the glowing fungus, the layered dust, the wooden paths). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong in the Luca and Lysana thread. Prose Control Moderate (the stacked similes in paragraph 49, the body images, and the slogan ending).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 25 to 29. It returns to the Pass team after the long Stormhaven run and is the first chapter in a while with room to breathe. It runs the "brief" and "execute" beats, with the poisoning plan as the turn. It is the lightest chapter in tone since the early Pass chapters, and it needs to be, because the next one is the poisoning.

**POP** Taerel, Luca, Lysana and Aymir yes, strongly. Brehn is a name and a line, thin by design. The Joblins and the orcs read as setting, which is right.

**AI** Light. The tells are the stacked weather similes (paragraphs 49, 50 and 174), body images for stone and cave (paragraphs 55 and 132), a not-X turn in paragraphs 8 and 131, a telling line in paragraph 105, and the slogan ending in paragraph 181. The dialogue is clean.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line and ran the mechanical net. The chapter has no stored Zac notes and no simile entry. I compared Aymir's whereabouts against the timeline in paragraphs 1 to 150, the vials against the plan, the Joblins against Chapters 22 and 25, Brehn and the allied soldiers against the ledger, and the lore in paragraphs 4 to 6 against the shards question from Chapter 31. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule. Ogres, the Luca and Weslin bond, the tunnel creatures and the civic seal are not in the ledger and are logged as questions.

# Chapter 38


## First impression

This is the Drake chapter, one long ninth night in Opindale, and it is the book's best look at a good man being squeezed. The opening is strong. The feast "burns" below the window, the dagger sits in its violet box, and Cotter's calm answer to "Does it kill?" is "It does not kill, Governor. It replaces." That is a line a reader will carry into the next chapters. The balcony beat ("He stood there until he was empty and then until he was decided") and the stray line "A stage for dancers who didn't know the play was ending" show Zac's voice at its best. The weak spots are the count of days, which disagrees with itself three ways, and a lot of repeated mood. Drake feels like a ghost five times, a funeral twice, alone three times, and the threat is stated at P13, P74 and P97. The roof watcher is a good device, but one line of narration steps out of Drake's head to count his victims. Several details also collide with Chapter 36, including how many children Drake has and whether Cotter's name is spelled right. The chapter ends on a held breath, a tic the book has used too often.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the window, the visit, the walk, the ball, the roof, the dance, the arch). Voice Differentiation Strong for Drake and Cotter, with the steward's calm menace the best of it. Stress Escalation Strong (the visit, the ballroom, the dance). World Texture Strong (the Accord, the statues, the delegates and their deals). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong in Drake's quiet scenes. Prose Control Moderate (the ghost, funeral and alone tics, and the held-breath ending).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 1 and 24, where Drake and Cotter appear. This is the first chapter told wholly from Drake's head and the first that shows the summit. It runs the "brief" beat for the next stretch, with the dagger as the turn and the dance as the pause before it. It is the most interior chapter of the book so far and it stands apart from the team chapters on purpose.

**POP** Drake and Cotter yes, strongly. Edric and Mirelle read as a couple worth losing. The roof watcher is a presence, and left unnamed on purpose.

**AI** Moderate. The tells are the ghost, funeral and alone motifs, the not-X turns (paragraphs 14, 42 and 88), the held-breath ending and the stock "worst part" line. The dialogue is clean.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line, ran the mechanical net, and applied Zac's stored notes (Colton to Cotter in ten places, Wyman to Wymark in paragraph 58, and the day count as a question). I compared the family list against Chapter 36, the steward's name and the dagger against the canon ledger, and the new names against the ledger, and I did not decide Drake's first name or the children. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule.

# Chapter 39


## First impression

This is the poisoning chapter, and it is the most fun the book has had in a while. Luca's infiltration works because it keeps almost going wrong, with the dropped orb on the rim, the cook's cleaver over his head and the Goblin thrall who just stands there and, to Luca's lasting regret, relieves himself. "I got held up, and pissed on. Not in that order" is the line that makes the scene. The long wait on the ridge is the book's warmest ensemble stretch, with the spoon-and-fork story, "Shadow finally found himself a candle" and Lysana's "Start thinking about how it begins". The turn is clean. Just as the poison works and the camp falls, the ground opens and the Joblins pour out, and the chapter's quiet theme, that the orcs' discipline was a screen for the digging, comes due. The problems are mostly bookkeeping. The poisons Luca carries and the poisons Chapter 37 laid out are not the same set, the ale is on the wrong side of the camp, and the soldier count has drifted from the ledger. The chapter also states its main idea about the orcs' cracks three times, pads the wait with a second round of Dorn stories, and uses the held breath again. Zac's three simile cuts are applied as Option A.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the infiltration, the long wait, the volleys, the walk down, the ground opening). Voice Differentiation Strong for Luca, Lysana, Aymir and Taerel, with the banter doing the work. Stress Escalation Strong (the dropped orb, the patrol, the poison, the Joblins). World Texture Strong (the camp, the thralls, the cauldron and the meat table). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong in the Luca and Lysana beats. Prose Control Moderate (the held breath, the repeated cracks, the padded wait and the not-X turns).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 25 and 37, the Pass chapters. It is the payoff of the plan laid out in Chapter 37 and the hinge of the Pass thread, and it runs the "execute" and "adapt" beats in one pass. It is the most action in a Pass chapter since Chapter 25 and the funniest.

**POP** Luca, Lysana, Aymir and Taerel yes, strongly. Dorn, Mira, Fenrick, Halden and Brant each have a line or a trait, which is what a roll call of grit needs. The orcs and Goblins read as a machine, and the Joblins as a surprise, which is right.

**AI** Light to Moderate. The tells are the held breath, the repeated cracks, the padded wait, the not-X turns (paragraphs 158 and 163) and the stock "almost surgical" line. The dialogue is clean.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line, ran the mechanical net, and applied Zac's stored notes (the heading, and the three simile cuts as Option A in his own replacement text). I compared the poisons, the ale, the soldier count and the tunnel against Chapter 37 and the canon ledger. Kingspit and Red Thrall are not in the ledger and are logged for it. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule.

# Chapter 40


## First impression

This is the chapter the Pass thread has been walking toward, and it hits hard. The Joblin tide, the Blackfire orbs, the twelve orcs that stand back up, and Fenrick's death are fast and bloody, and the action reads clearly because Zac keeps the beats short and the sounds loud. Lysana's death is the heart of it. It is not a clean beat, since she is stabbed in the neck, has a few seconds, and smiles. Luca's reaction is the right one, a man who does not scream and moves instead, then stops. Aymir's "No, no no no" and Taerel who "didn't breathe" are the best secondary notes. The darkness when Luca pulls everything from the shard is the scariest passage in the book so far, because it is mostly sound. The last line, "I did.", is quiet and exactly right. The chapter works because nothing is explained. The problems are small. Taerel has two orbs and then a "last one" after two throws. The darkness falls on a "grove" in a valley camp, and a goblet is dropped on a stone floor in the middle of a battlefield. The chapter says Taerel "had never seen death up close" about a man who has fought orcs. The prose uses "death" as a stock word five times in a page and leans on the same phrases for the swarm. Nothing here needs a rewrite, and the death scene should be trimmed, not rebuilt.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the swarm, the orbs, the rising twelve, the death, the dark, the silence). Voice Differentiation Strong for Luca, Aymir, Taerel, Dorn and Lysana's last look. Stress Escalation Strong. World Texture Strong. Sensory Grounding Strong, with the sound passage the best in the book. Emotional Subtext Strong in the death and Aymir's grief. Prose Control Moderate (the stock "death" word, the held-breath wind, the stacked "didn't" lines).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 25, 37 and 39, the Pass thread. This is its climax and the book's first death of a main team member. It runs the "execute" and "adapt" beats, with the shard pull as the turn. It is the shortest chapter in lines and the heaviest in effect, and the last line is as quiet as the middle is loud.

**POP** Luca, Aymir, Taerel and Lysana yes, strongly. Dorn, Mira, Halden and Brant yes, with Fenrick's death landing because he was seventeen and half listening. The Joblins and the orcs read as a tide.

**AI** Light to Moderate. The tells are the stock use of "death", the wind that forgets how to breathe, the not-X turns (paragraphs 76, 124 and 138), the stray curdled-milk phrase and the repeated swarm lines. The dialogue is clean.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line and ran the mechanical net. The chapter has no stored Zac notes and no simile entry. I compared the orb count against Chapter 37 and the plan, Luca's shard against Chapter 39 and the canon ledger, Taerel's wound and history against Chapters 37 and 39, and the civilians against Chapter 39. I did not explain what the shard released, since the ledger records that as Zac's ruling. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule. The inferno plate and the goblet are not in the ledger and are logged as questions.

# Chapter 41


## First impression

This is Riven and Nyssa's chapter, and it is a gift. The first half is a long walk and talk on a mountain ledge that pays off a decade of history. Riven finally says "Why is it never me?", Nyssa says "Because I can't lose you", and he gives her his blessing for Dain in a speech that costs him. "I think he'd be good for you. If you let him" is the line that makes the scene. The second half is a caper, and it is a good one. The empty statue, the hidden bolt-hole, the "stashy-stash", the rappel race, the half-plate mercs, the shaft Nyssa remembers from a drunk night and the vent that is "always a tight fit" all show two people who have done this for years. The banter ("Define cheating", "Loser buys the next round", "Flexible truth") is the best two-hander in the book. The problem is that Riven and Nyssa have the same conversation three times, on the ledge, at the statue and in the bolt-hole, and Nyssa says "I might stay", "give him a chance" and "I want you in it" in nearly the same words each time. She even jokes about the "hard sell" herself, which helps, but the middle talk is the weakest of the three. The speeches also sometimes explain the feelings the scene has already shown. A handful of details clash with Chapter 36, mainly the keys, the vault and the statue. The dialogue is typed with straight marks throughout, which needs a global fix. Zac's one Keep, the "words ran out" line, stays.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the climb, the ledge, the statue, the bolt-hole, the vault fight, the shaft, the vent). Voice Differentiation Strong for Riven and Nyssa, who are the best banter pair in the book. Stress Escalation Strong in the vault. World Texture Strong (the Builder's Cache, the shaft, the vent). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong on the ledge. Prose Control Moderate (the repeated conversation, the ghost, the explained feelings).

**COMPARE** Against Chapters 34 and 36, where Riven and Nyssa are part of the group. This is their chapter, and it is the first to give Riven a full scene and the first to resolve his jealousy of Dain from Chapter 36. It runs the "execute" and "adapt" beats, with the empty statue as the turn. It is the warmest chapter since Chapter 37 and has the best caper in the book.

**POP** Riven and Nyssa yes, strongly. The mercenaries read as a function. Dain is present only through what the two say about him, which suits the chapter.

**AI** Light to Moderate. The tells are the ghost image, the stock "hit like a hammer", the explained feelings, and the closing stock lines. The dialogue is clean and, where it is not explaining, very good.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line and ran the mechanical net. The one stored Zac note is the Keep on paragraph 116, which I left as written, and any trimming advice keeps that line. I compared the statue and the vault against Chapter 36, the half-plate against Chapter 37, and Riven's later fate and the tower plans against the canon ledger. Dunlow, Ironvale, Mr. Hogan and Lady Veyra are not in the ledger and are logged for it. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule.

# Chapter 42


## First impression

This chapter is built like a heist and it works. The dawn huddle sets the stakes, the split into three teams is clear, and the Merrick manor sequence is the most fun Reau and Riven have had together. The Keryn meeting is the best scene in it. "Define 'live'", "carrying more silence than armor" and "the blade that makes him bleed" give her a voice in four minutes, and the cellar, the study, the false vault and the trapped case move fast. The market ending is the real prize. A city of people turning in silence to face one cart, with only the snow still moving, is a great closing image and the Havern Ball banter just before it makes the drop harder. The chapter's problems are small and mostly about the plan. The team is told twice to meet at Blackcap Alley and then Weslin announces a different order. The hunt for a key gives way to a case with no lock. The scene leaves at night and arrives at midday. And the place names around Merrick (Ember Hill, Stormhaven, Forgehallow) do not agree with the ledger. The prose carries a few stock images in the tense stretches, mostly the clock-mechanism woman, "something older than that" and the weather chill. Zac's Keep on Riven stopping after four paces stays exactly as written.

# Chapter 43


## First impression

This is the tower team's approach chapter, and it is the strongest "plan, brief, execute, adapt" run since the Pass. Garr's crew moves like people who have done this before. Nyssa kills without a sound, Ash and Aldrek take the third man, Neavin's falcon scouts, and the moldy bread "still arranged with care" says everything about the city in four words. Aurelia's seizure is the set piece, and it earns it. The accent "that didn't quite belong", the babble about veils and cracks in the firmament, then the whole district freezing to listen is the best creep in the book so far. The puzzle-door sequence that closes the chapter is a good team beat. The lock, the collapse, the key, the hidden seam and the four columns turn into a trust exercise, and "Let the stone tell you" is a fine line for Aldrek. Two things hold it back. The chapter explains the tower twice (the opening paragraphs and again in paragraphs 25 and 26), and the pep talk to Ash runs on too long, with Ash arguing the same point three times and Garr repeating the exit plan twice. A few lines of the puzzle also say the same thing more than once, and the lock chain leaves a second key lying unused. Some of the dialogue drops its contractions and reads stiffly. The prose carries a handful of stock beats ("it was a message", "a scream that would haunt the dead", "That felt earned"). The Dain and Nyssa moment at the lock is a quiet payoff of Chapter 41 and works. Aurelia's voice stays unstable, as locked.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the approach, the goodbye, the kills, the seizure, the argument, the lock, the columns). Voice Differentiation Strong for Ash, Aldrek and Dain, Moderate for Nyssa in the formal lines. Stress Escalation Strong at Aurelia's seizure. World Texture Strong (the moldy bread, the false groove, the dwarven columns). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong in the Dain and Nyssa beat. Prose Control Moderate (the double description, the repeated beats, the stock lines).

**COMPARE** Against Chapter 41's caper and Chapter 42's heist, this is the third panel of the day, the straight-ahead strike. It is more tense and less funny, and the puzzle sequence is its heist. It has the best ensemble work of the three chapters, with every member of the strike team getting a beat.

**POP** Garr, Nyssa, Ash, Dain and Aldrek yes. Neavin and Aurelia are mostly function until the seizure, and Aurelia lands there. The Red Cloaks are bodies, which is the point of the opening.

**AI** Light to Moderate. The tells are the not-X turns, the beat-marker lines, "The show must go on", "That felt earned" and the repeated tower description. The dialogue is clean and, where it is not explaining, very good.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line and ran the mechanical net. There are no stored Zac notes for this chapter. I compared the tower's numbers against the canon ledger (thirty-five floors, four sub-basements), the Red Cloaks and Adepts against the Veydrassil entry, Harmon's errand against Chapter 42, and Aurelia's possession against the locked "no stable true voice" fact. I name no one as the speaker in the possession and make no claim about Harmon's fate. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule.

# Chapter 44


## First impression

This is the descent chapter, and it is the creepiest one in the book. The team climbs through the tower's lower levels, the dwarven gauntlet keeps turning on them, and the mindless civilians are everywhere, each stuck in one small task. The butcher sharpening a cleaver "back and forth", the child mending a net with fingers that never slow, the blacksmith whose hammer "never strikes true" and the woman who folds the same cloths again and again do more than any monster. Ash's growing headache, the humming rods in the stone and Aldrek's line "The stone is speaking, but not to us" give the climb a clear spine. Aldrek's reading of the civilians as a sentence rather than obedience is the most interesting idea in the chapter. The empty prison with its one clean silver plate is a great image, the dockworker's scream is the right kind of shock, and the voice in the skull gives the fight an extra layer of dread. "That was new" in paragraph 97 is the best line in the book for what it says about this team. The chapter's problems are small and mostly about details. Ash's headache is described as unspoken after he has spoken of it twice, the gate to the prison is barred and then slammed shut, the cells are open and then not, and the tower's level count does not add up. The prose leans on a few repeated phrases ("not just cold", "sentence", "puppet") and a stock villain voice. The loudspeaker simile is a modern image in a world without them.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the stairs, the loop, the corridor, the forge door, the levels, the prison, the fight, the Adept). Voice Differentiation Strong for Aldrek, Ash and Dain. Stress Escalation Strong from the scream onward. World Texture Strong (the civilians, the rods, the plate, the cells). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong in Ash's silence and "That was new". Prose Control Moderate (the repeated motifs, the stock villain, the loudspeaker).

**COMPARE** Against Chapter 43's approach, this chapter is the descent into the thing itself. It is the most atmospheric of the three chapters in the tower and has the best horror writing in the book. The gauntlet is longer than it needs to be, but each station is a different kind of wrong.

**POP** Aldrek, Ash and Nyssa yes. Dain is function in the fight, which suits the chapter. The civilians read as one body and are the best creepy detail in the book. The voice is a presence and not a character.

**AI** Light to Moderate. The tells are the not-X turns, the loudspeaker, the repeated "not just cold", the rag simile and the stock closer. The horror is clean and specific, and the dialogue is good.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line and ran the mechanical net. There are no stored Zac notes for this chapter. I compared the tower's level count against the ledger and Chapter 43, the collar against Chapter 42, and the civilians against Chapters 41 to 43. I name no speaker for the voice and draw no link to the possession in Chapter 43. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule, including Aldrek's prayer and his purgatory image.

# Chapter 45


## First impression

This is the chapter where the tower talks. The fight with the Adept and his six Red Cloaks is the book's best set piece for pure teamwork. Ash holds the fire shield to the point of breaking, Aldrek's white wall backs him, Dain and Nyssa wait for the drop, and the moment the shield shatters they go in together. Then the book slows down on purpose. The looting (ball bearings, firestones, a water flask passed round) is small and human, and Ash taking the Adept's shard from a body he does not yet know is Talron's brother is a quiet piece of staging. The interrogation is the real prize. Talron's "My name's Talron. It always has been" and Nyssa's "Why the second part?" turn a captured soldier into a person in four lines. His account of the Garrison commander opening the gates, the men in strange armor, the black box for the tower's crown, the gate below Unity Square and the voice behind the thoughts hands the reader the biggest block of plot since the Pass, and it is mostly well paced. Aldrek's attempt to loosen the hold on Talron's mind ("There are cracks") is a lovely, unfussy beat. The weak points are small. The narration names Talron before he names himself, Dain loses his voice and then speaks, some of Talron's directions contradict each other (the stair "at the lowest level" turns up in the Grand Floor kitchen, bindings that never come off, a threat he never made), and a handful of stock lines sit on strong beats. The ending, where Talron walks off into the dark with a smile and a reminder, is a good unsettling cliffhanger. I name no one as Korr and say nothing about what he is.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the fight, the shield, the looting, the interrogation, the infiltration, the exit). Voice Differentiation Strong for Talron, Ash and Aldrek. Stress Escalation Strong in the fight. World Texture Strong (the shard, the box, the gate, the beast). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong in the name beat and the brother. Prose Control Moderate (the early naming, the stock lines).

**COMPARE** Against Chapter 44's descent, this chapter is the answer and the exposition. It carries the most plot of the three tower chapters and the best character writing. Talron is the strongest one-chapter character since the Pass.

**POP** Talron yes, strongly. Ash, Aldrek and Nyssa yes. Dain is function in the fight and stronger in the interrogation. The Red Cloaks are bodies, apart from the Adept who becomes a brother.

**AI** Light to Moderate. The tells are the not-X turns, the stock closing lines and the early naming. The dialogue is clean and the exposition is mostly hidden inside a person.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line and ran the mechanical net. There are no stored Zac notes for this chapter. I compared the tower's floors, the Unity Square entry, the beast and Veydrassil against the ledger, Talron against his ledger entry, and the voice against Chapters 43 and 44. I name no one as Korr and say nothing about what Korr is, in line with the open decision. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule.

# Chapter 46


## First impression

This is Harmon's chapter, and it is the one the book has been building toward since the prison. A student he trained comes back with sabers and a reason, and the fight in the loft is the best one-on-one in the story. It is mean and uneven, it goes through the ring armor and the broken helm, and it works because both men are right and wrong at once. Torn's grief is real, Harmon's account of the fallback order is plausible, and neither version is allowed to win. Then Weslin's kill lands. The illusion, the dagger, the ringing behind his eyes, "I didn't know it would feel like that", and the squire's oath that comes out of him unplanned are the emotional peak of the book so far. Harmon's "The weight you're feeling right now is what separates you from what we just put in the ground" is the right line for the right moment. The second half is a handoff chapter with a sting. The cart ride, the name on the page, the missing children, Garr's retelling of Aurelia at the tower and Harmon's cane and his "let me speak to it first" are all good plants, and the violet bolt closes it on a hook. The weak points are mostly seams. The opening dagger beat is garbled, the narrator switches between "Torn" and "Teralon" mid-scene, Torn's confession names setbacks the reader never saw, and Garr's retelling of the tower voice does not match Chapter 43. Garr's place also finally settles, since he is outside here and the earlier chapters disagree. Four of Zac's simile cuts fall in this chapter and are applied as written. The same template ("the way a man...") shows up in other lines Zac did not flag, and I note them as options. Neavin's dialect in paragraph 166 is intentional and stays.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the lesson, the ambush, the duel, the kill, the oath, the ride, the briefing, the bolt). Voice Differentiation Strong for Harmon, Torn and Weslin, and Neavin's dialect holds. Stress Escalation Strong in the duel. World Texture Strong (the loft, the missing children, the pond). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong in the oath and the kill. Prose Control Moderate (the "the way" template, the seams, the retelling).

**COMPARE** Against Chapter 27, where Torn rides off, and Chapter 23, where he is freed, this chapter pays off his arc and gives Weslin the most important beat of his own. It is the best-built chapter since the Pass and the first in the book where the two halves (the duel and the ride) each carry their own weight. The tower chapters give it a sting, since the voice that scares the team there is the thing Harmon says he knows.

**POP** Harmon, Torn and Weslin yes, strongly. Reau and Riven work as a pair in the ride. Garr and Neavin are solid. Aurelia is a presence from a distance.

**AI** Light to Moderate. The tells are the "the way a man..." template (applied as Zac's cuts in four places, with three more options), the "older than" turn, and a few stock closers. The dialogue is clean and the fight is specific.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line and ran the mechanical net. Zac's four simile notes are applied as written (three Finds as Option A with his replacement text, one deletion). I checked Torn and Weslin's arcs against the ledger, the violet shard and the cane against the plants, and Garr's retelling against Chapter 43. Garr's place is noted as settled here and the earlier chapters are marked. I name no one as the speaker of the voice in the tower. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule, including Harmon's silent prayer and Torn's "Your gods won't save you".

# Chapter 47


## First impression

This is the climb chapter, and it is the strongest piece of sustained dread in the book. The team goes up through the tower floor by floor, and each floor is wrong in a new way. The abandoned throne room is kept like a tomb someone still visits, the servant quarters hold a pair of boots "placed", not tossed, the crates are too big to have come up any stair, the barracks floor is nothing but empty armor with a boot "still tied" in a double knot, and the gear is warm. Aldrek's "The tower. It hurts." and "Because some paths are meant to be walked only once" are two of the best lines he has had. Ash's jokes ("Big chair. Bet the view was great.") keep the dread from going flat. Nyssa's recognition of the governor's sister-in-law is a clean hook, and the trap that follows is a good one. Her hesitation over the mimic child ("Her hands disagreed by about a quarter-second") is the best character beat in the fight. The flesh golem is a fair brawl and the end, with something non-human hitting the door, is a good cliffhanger. The weak points are small. The geography of the thirty-second floor is hard to follow, since the reader meets the sister-in-law twice in two places. The execution is "within the hour" when the bells say two hours, the narration says "an hour ago" for something minutes old, and a few new names (Stormhaven Armistice, Hollow Spine) are not in my notes. The prose has a run of not-X turns, and Aldrek's lecture on the tower sounds like a guidebook. The one stored Zac cut (Aldrek and the nail) is applied as written, and "Tarnished" stays. An unsourced note about the mimic family needs Zac's confirmation, and I add nothing for it.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the climb, the throne room, the empty floors, the barracks, the guards, the chamber, the trap, the golem). Voice Differentiation Strong for Ash, Aldrek and Nyssa. Prose Control Moderate (the not-X turns, the floor geography, the clock).

**COMPARE** Against Chapter 44's descent, this chapter is the same tower seen from the other end, up instead of down. It is warmer in light and colder in feeling, and the empty-armor floor is the creepiest single room in the book. The fight is shorter and plainer than Chapter 45's, which suits it.

**POP** Ash, Aldrek and Nyssa yes. Dain works as the point man. The mimics and the golem read as function, which is right. The sister-in-law is a presence, not a character, which is the point.

**AI** Moderate in the middle (a run of not-X turns and "older than" phrases), light elsewhere. The dialogue is clean and the physical detail is specific.

# Chapter 48


## First impression

This is the escape chapter, and the engine of it is good. Korr's astral projection bursting through the windows is a strong cold open, the sealed door "that was not there before" is a clean creepy beat, and Aldrek's summoned guardian is the best use of his faith in the book. The wind-catch shaft pays off the crates from Chapter 47. Ash talking the boy through the jump is warm, and Dain's dry summary of what Aldrek did ("with a limp arm and then taking a bolt down a shaft for the privilege") is a gift. The bell countdown that closes the chapter, one chime per beat while the three groups split, is the best structural device in the last act. The weak points are fixable. The cost of Korr's projection is stated five times. Several cart and character assignments disagree with each other (Briala is called the boy's mother, Ash rides alone beside a cart he is guarding, Aurelia and Neavin change carts on the page). The split is announced twice. The carts wait on a rise in one paragraph and in a grain passage in the next. Harmon's recognition scene (the crowned figure) tells his backstory in four overlapping gestures ("a different era", "under a different sky", "over centuries", "thirty years"), and one of those lines states what Korr is to the crowned figure, so I log it as a question and add nothing. Zac's three stored simile cuts are applied as written. Nothing here changes who Korr is or who the crowned figure is.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the burst, the sprint, the seal, the guardian, the shaft, the courtyard, the ride, the bells). Voice Differentiation Strong for Ash, Aldrek, Dain and Nyssa, Moderate for Harmon's interior. Stress Escalation Strong through the courtyard and the bell sequence. World Texture Strong (the shaft, the dome, the sashes, the warbeast). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong in Ash and the boy. Prose Control Moderate (the repeated cost of the projection, the cart assignments, Harmon's backstory hints).

**COMPARE** Against Chapter 47's climb, this is the exit, down instead of up, and it moves faster. The shaft and the courtyard run are the best set pieces, and the closing chimes are the cleanest ending in the last act.

**POP** Ash, Aldrek, Dain, Nyssa and Briala yes. Riven and Reau are lean and sharp. Garr is a sniper, which reads as function. Harmon's interior is the weakest voice, since it tells where the others show.

**AI** Moderate in the middle (not-X turns, repeated cost lines, stock closers), light in the dialogue. The Harmon passage carries the heaviest cluster.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line and ran the mechanical net. Zac's three stored simile cuts are applied as written. The unsourced mimic-family note and the Aurelia placement note are logged as questions with nothing added. I checked the family relations against the ledger (Briala is Karethiel's sister), the cart assignments against paragraphs 229 and 244, and the bell count against Chapters 45 and 47. I state nothing about what Korr or the crowned figure is. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule, including Aldrek's prayer and "I swear on God's mercy".

# Chapter 49


## First impression

This is the chapter where the book changes rooms, and it earns the change. The seven-clank countdown (one memory, one clank, then the blade) is the cleanest piece of structure in the back half. It mirrors the bell sequence that closes Chapter 48, so the two chapters rhyme without saying so. Drake's failed attack is tight, and Edric's "Don't trust your closest friends" note is a very good hook. The Mirelle balcony scene is the strongest writing in the chapter. Her control over the assassin is real menace, and "Men are so easy to manipulate" followed by a kiss with her husband sets up a marriage that is both love and strategy. The feast vignettes (Sola Drey, Factor Jeld, Lord Colven) are lively and plant the north. The old man and the changeling closing the chapter are the right kind of creepy, and the countess's "the king rarely wanders far without his crown" plus Edric's "some eggs must break" memory is a very good turn on a character the reader likes. There are three real continuity problems. Chapter 48 ends with Harmon deciding "not tonight" on sending word, and here his message arrives within minutes and says the family is "with me now" when the family rides in Garr's cart. The bell is called "the first bell" in a chapter whose anchor is the seventh. Drake is sent to the room where the Steward is hiding. The Mirelle scene has a run of subtext-explaining lines that tell what the dialogue already shows, and the old man's thoughts repeat Chapter 48's habit of vague "last time" gestures. Zac's four stored simile cuts are applied as written. The ledger's open question on the seventh-bell anchor is answered, and the connecting line is on the page. I say nothing about who the old man or the changeling is.

## Chapter wrap

**GRAIN** Cadence Variety Strong (the clank structure, the balcony, the corridor vignettes, the old man, the countess). Voice Differentiation Strong for Edric, Mirelle, Drake and Jeld. Stress Escalation Strong in the clank sequence. World Texture Strong (the feast, the named nations, the factors). Sensory Grounding Strong. Emotional Subtext Strong in the Edric and Mirelle marriage scene, Moderate where the narrator explains it. Prose Control Moderate (the explained subtext, the stacked vague backstory).

**COMPARE** Against Chapter 48's escape, this is the same night from the other end of the map, still, indoors and talk-driven, and the structure rhymes with the bells. It is a long chapter and the middle (the corridor vignettes) is the slackest stretch, though each vignette plants something or sells the court.

**POP** Edric, Mirelle, Drake and Sola Drey yes. Jeld and Colven read as sketches, which suits their size. The old man is vague on purpose. The changeling is a function, which is right.

**AI** Moderate in the Mirelle scene (explained subtext, stock similes), light elsewhere. The dialogue and the clank sequence are clean.

**METHOD** I read the whole chapter line by line and ran the mechanical net. Zac's four stored simile cuts are applied as written, and the locked spellings are corrected. The unsourced timeline note is answered, since the seventh-bell line is on the page. I compared Harmon's message against Chapter 48 (the cart split and his "not tonight" thought) and the place names against the ledger (all canon). I name no identity for the old man or the changeling. I left every religious reference as written, per the God stays rule, including "God the Creator" in paragraph 97.

# Chapter 50


## First impression

This is the landing after the pass battle, and it is a quiet, strong chapter. After four chapters of Stormhaven noise, it hands the book to Aymir and Taerel in the snow with Lysana's body on the third horse, and it lets them grieve without a speech. The brothers' talk is the heart of it. The three roads home, ship work and the old thieving trade are real choices with real costs, and Aymir's "I didn't like all of who I was in it. But I liked not guessing who I should be" is the best line either brother has. The coin in the sunrise is a good small image, and the laugh over "Dad" at the end earns its warmth. Corren's account of the changeling is the plot payload, and it lands as horror because the smell ("sweet, like overripe fruit ... and underneath it, oil") is concrete. The weak points are specific. Aymir recalls Corren's description at paragraph 49, long before they meet him. The slogan is counted as "Seven words" and it has six. The pass team's thread returns with no time anchor after four Stormhaven chapters. The brothers' talk runs about thirty paragraphs and restates its options once, and silence is described four times. The "filed it away" motif runs three times in the inserted passages. Zac's five stored notes are handled as written (three cuts, two Keeps), and the Brotherhood leader with three fingers gone is left unexplained per the open decision. I say nothing about who or what Korr is.
